interview_metadata.name: John Garrity
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) — Full 109 questions
interview_metadata.interview_note: Participant is a 2-year-old child. Interview conducted as a proxy interview with John's mother (Sarah Garrity) responding on his behalf, with direct quotes and observed behavior from John recorded where applicable. John was present throughout, playing with blocks on the living room floor.

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: [Mother, Sarah, answering for John] Well, John's whole life IS his childhood — he just turned two in March. He was born right here in Kennewick at Trios Health Hospital, full term, healthy. My husband Mark and I had been trying for a while, so John was very much wanted. The first year was a blur — colic until about four months, then he became this giggly, observant baby. He started walking at thirteen months, talking around fifteen, and by eighteen months he was already obsessed with sorting things. Blocks by color, his little toy cars by size, even his cheerios by — I don't know, some internal logic only he understands. He started at Little Sprouts Learning Center part-time last September, three mornings a week. That was a big transition. The major life event so far was probably the move — we moved from a small apartment near Vista Field into our current house on Olympia Street when John was about ten months old. He has the corner bedroom with the window facing the backyard. He's the only child right now. [John interjects: 'Mama! Blue!' — holding up a blue block] Yes, baby, that's blue. Good job. See, that's pretty much his life — blocks, books, the park, and Bluey.

follow_ups.question: What was the move like for him?
follow_ups.response: He was young enough that he adjusted within about two weeks. The first few nights he was confused — kept toddling toward where his crib used to be. We kept the same bedtime routine, same blanket, same bedtime book (Goodnight Moon), and that smoothed it out. Mark and I learned early: change the place, keep the rituals.

follow_ups.question: What's a typical morning look like for John?
follow_ups.response: He wakes up around 6:30 — earlier than we'd like. He calls 'Mama, up!' from his crib. We do diaper, then he wants 'milky' which is whole milk in his blue sippy cup. Breakfast is usually banana with peanut butter or oatmeal. Then it's either Little Sprouts on Monday, Wednesday, Friday mornings, or stay-home days with me on Tuesdays and Thursdays where we do library storytime or the splash pad in summer.

follow_ups.question: Has he had any health scares?
follow_ups.response: One ear infection in January, otherwise just the usual toddler colds. He's right on his growth curves. The pediatrician at Kadlec Pediatrics, Dr. Reyes, is wonderful with him.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: [Mother] For John, the closest thing to a crossroads was the decision about daycare versus staying home. I was working part-time at the Mid-Columbia Library before John was born, and we genuinely went back and forth on whether I'd quit or whether we'd put him in full-time care. We landed on a middle path — Little Sprouts three mornings, me with him the other days. I think that decision shaped him a lot. He's social enough at Little Sprouts that he doesn't melt down around other kids, but he also still has these quiet structured days at home where he can do his sorting and his block towers without interruption. If we'd gone full-time daycare, I think he'd be a different kid — maybe more boisterous, maybe less into the order-loving stuff. If I'd stayed home full-time, he probably wouldn't share his toys as easily as he does now.

follow_ups.question: How did you decide?
follow_ups.response: Honestly, we made a spreadsheet. Mark works at Energy Northwest — he's in operations support — and his schedule is rigid. Mine was flexible. We looked at finances, looked at three daycares, and Little Sprouts had the smallest toddler room and the warmest director. That tipped it.

follow_ups.question: Do you ever second-guess it?
follow_ups.response: On the days I drop him off and he cries — yes. But by the time I pick him up at noon he's painting at an easel and barely waves goodbye to his teacher. So no, not really.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: [Mother] Very conscious. Mark and I are spreadsheet people. We don't really let big things 'just happen' if we can help it. Even John's bedtime routine was workshopped — we read three books on toddler sleep before we settled on ours.

follow_ups.question: Is that personality something John seems to be picking up?
follow_ups.response: Oh, absolutely. He lines his shoes up by the door. He's two. He gets very upset if the cereal bowl is the wrong color. So yes — conscious choosing is genetic in this house, apparently.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: [Mother] My mom flew in from Spokane for the first month after John was born, which was a lifesaver. And the Benton-Franklin Health District has a free home-visit program for new parents — a nurse came twice. Beyond that, we were pretty self-sufficient. Mark's parents are in Boise so they visit a few times a year.

follow_ups.question: Was there anything you wished had been available?
follow_ups.response: More flexible part-time daycare options. Most places want either full-time or nothing — finding a three-morning slot took six months of waitlists.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: [Mother] For John, family is Mark and me first — Daddy and Mama. He has very strong opinions about which of us does what. Bath time is Daddy's job, and if I try to step in he says 'No, Daddy do it.' Bedtime stories are mine. He has my mom — he calls her 'Gramma Linda' — she FaceTimes him almost every other day from Spokane and he absolutely lights up. He has Mark's parents, who he calls 'Papa and Nana,' and they come down for Thanksgiving and Easter and his birthday. He has one cousin, Mia, who's four — she's my sister Rachel's daughter, also in Spokane. They see each other maybe six times a year and Mia bosses him around in a way he tolerates surprisingly well. That's pretty much John's circle of family.

follow_ups.question: How does he show affection?
follow_ups.response: Big squishy hugs around the legs. He's a leg-hugger. And he gives kisses on demand — but only on the cheek, and only if you ask nicely. He calls Mark 'Daddy-boy' sometimes, which we have no idea where it came from.

follow_ups.question: Any siblings on the horizon?
follow_ups.response: We're talking about it. Probably try for a second next year. John doesn't really have the concept yet — when I point at pregnant women he just says 'lady big.'

follow_ups.question: How often does he see his cousin Mia?
follow_ups.response: About every other month. We drive up to Spokane or they come down. They overlap at Christmas, Easter, July 4th, and a summer cabin weekend at Lake Coeur d'Alene.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: [Mother] My brother David lives in Seattle — he's an uncle but they don't see each other much, maybe twice a year. Mark has one brother in Boise too, Uncle Tim. That's about it.

follow_ups.question: Does John have a favorite?
follow_ups.response: Uncle Tim, no contest — Tim does the airplane-spin game when he visits.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: [Mother] His best 'friends' are his Little Sprouts classmates — there's a little girl named Ellie he plays parallel-blocks with, and a boy named Marcus who he chases at the playground. His teacher, Miss Jenna, is probably the most important non-family adult in his life right now. He talks about her on weekends — 'Miss Jenna, song?' He also adores the children's librarian at the Kennewick Branch, Miss Patty, who runs Tuesday storytime. And our neighbors, the Hoangs, have a daughter Lily who's three — they play in the backyard most weekends.

follow_ups.question: How often does he see Lily?
follow_ups.response: Probably three or four times a week — they share a fence and we've made a little gate between the yards. It's been a godsend.

follow_ups.question: Does he have a favorite adult outside family?
follow_ups.response: Miss Jenna. He drew her a 'picture' last week — just scribbles, but he was very serious about it. He carried it to school like it was an offering.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: [Mother] We're in the Creekstone area of south Kennewick, off Olympia Street. It's a newer development, maybe fifteen years old — mostly young families and some retirees. The houses are these tan stucco craftsman-style places, small yards, sidewalks, cul-de-sacs. We can walk to Lawrence Scott Park in about ten minutes — that's John's home base. There's a little neighborhood market called Yoke's a five-minute drive, and Costco is about ten. We're maybe twenty minutes from the Columbia River trail. Demographically it's pretty mixed — white, Hispanic, some Pacific Islander families. Almost everyone has kids or grandkids around.

follow_ups.question: What's it like during a typical Saturday morning?
follow_ups.response: Sprinklers, dogs, dads mowing lawns. Honestly idyllic in an almost embarrassing way. John toddles around in the driveway with sidewalk chalk while Mark washes the car.

follow_ups.question: Any neighborhood traditions?
follow_ups.response: There's a big Fourth of July block party every year — they shut down our cul-de-sac and one of the dads grills. Last year was John's first one and he was terrified of the sparklers.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: [Mother] Very safe. I let John play in the front yard with me sitting on the porch and don't think twice. There was one car break-in two streets over a year ago and the neighborhood Facebook group lost its mind about it for a week, which tells you what the baseline is.

follow_ups.question: Anything that does make you uneasy?
follow_ups.response: Traffic on Steptoe Street — people drive too fast through the cut-through. John knows 'stop at the curb' but I don't trust drivers.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: [Mother] Ups: schools are decent, parks are great, the river is right there, summers are dry. Downs: summers are also 105 degrees and smoky from wildfires the last few Augusts. The wildfire smoke last summer kept John indoors for almost two weeks straight, which was rough on everyone.

follow_ups.question: How did John handle the smoke days?
follow_ups.response: Lots of Bluey. We turned the living room into a 'fort camp.' He still asks to do 'fort day' when it rains.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: [Mother] It's the three of us — Mark, John, and me. Plus our cat, Biscuit, who John considers a sibling. No one else right now, though my mom stays in the guest room when she visits, usually one long week per quarter.

follow_ups.question: How does John get along with Biscuit?
follow_ups.response: Reverently. He says 'gentle pet' before touching her, which we drilled into him. Biscuit tolerates him.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: [Mother] All permanent. Just us three.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: [Mother] Just my mom, Linda, when she visits — usually one week every few months.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: [Mother] No, no one.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: [Mother] John's week is patterned. Monday, Wednesday, Friday mornings he's at Little Sprouts from 8:30 to noon. I pick him up, we have lunch — usually cheese pizza bites or mac and cheese — then he naps from 1 to 3. Afternoons are park, backyard, or playdates. Tuesday is library storytime at 10 a.m. at the Kennewick Branch. Thursday is grocery day — he 'helps' me at Yoke's, mostly putting things in the cart and back out again. Saturdays we usually do a family activity — Columbia River walk, splash pad in summer, or the Benton County library. Sundays are pancake mornings — Mark makes blueberry pancakes — and then we sometimes go to the 10 a.m. service at Bethel Church if we're feeling motivated.

follow_ups.question: What's his favorite day of the week?
follow_ups.response: Tuesday, hands down. Storytime is sacred. He picks out his 'library shirt' the night before — it's a yellow shirt with a giraffe.

follow_ups.question: Any TV or screen time in the routine?
follow_ups.response: About thirty minutes after lunch while I clean up — usually Bluey or Sesame Street. And maybe one show in the evening if dinner's running late.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: [Mother] John doesn't work — he's two. His 'job' is preschool three mornings a week. If you mean me, I work part-time as a library aide at Mid-Columbia Library District, about fifteen hours a week, mostly during John's Little Sprouts mornings. Mark works full-time at Energy Northwest in operations support, Monday through Friday, 7 a.m. to 4 p.m.

follow_ups.question: Does John know what 'work' means?
follow_ups.response: He thinks Mark 'goes to the 'lectricity place.' He waves at the power lines and says 'Daddy work.' That's his mental model.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: [Mother] John has 'chores' — air quotes. He puts his dirty clothes in the hamper, helps wipe his high chair tray, and 'feeds' Biscuit by handing me the scoop. He's responsible for putting his blocks away before bath — that's non-negotiable, and he does it. He also helps water the herb pots on the back deck with his little blue watering can on Saturday mornings.

follow_ups.question: Does he ever resist these tasks?
follow_ups.response: The block clean-up sometimes. We sing 'clean up, clean up' and that usually moves him. Bribery via raisins also works.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: [Mother] Two big ones recently. First, he started T-ball through the Kennewick Youth Soccer Club's 'Tiny Tots' program in April — Saturdays at 9 a.m. at Southridge Sports Complex. Second, we dropped his morning nap about two months ago — he's down to one afternoon nap. That shifted everything because mornings are now longer and busier.

follow_ups.question: How's T-ball going?
follow_ups.response: Hilarious. He stands at the tee, swings, and then runs to second base because that's where Daddy is cheering. They mostly just throw balls in random directions. He loves it.

follow_ups.question: Was dropping the morning nap rough?
follow_ups.response: Week one was brutal. Now he sleeps harder in the afternoon and goes down earlier at night, around 7.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: [Mother] John's not in school school yet, but a Little Sprouts day: drop-off at 8:30, circle time with songs, free play, snack at 9:30 (usually crackers and fruit), structured activity like painting or sensory bins, outside play at 11, pick-up at noon. After 'school' it's lunch, nap, then either playdate, park, or quiet time at home. T-ball Saturdays are his only structured 'after school' activity right now. Library storytime is his other regular outing.

follow_ups.question: Any other activities you're considering?
follow_ups.response: Swim lessons at the Toyota Center pool this summer, and probably a music class in the fall. We're trying not to over-schedule him.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: [Mother] John's experience with law enforcement is limited to waving at the police car that does the safety visit to Little Sprouts in October. He's fascinated by the lights. He calls it the 'whoo-whoo car.' Personally, Mark and I have had nothing beyond a speeding ticket each.

follow_ups.question: Has he ever interacted directly with an officer?
follow_ups.response: Officer Lopez came to the Little Sprouts safety event and let the kids sit in the cruiser. John was thrilled. He talked about it for a week.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: [Mother] Nothing else. We're pretty boring in that respect.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: [Mother] No. No one in our immediate family has been arrested.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: [Mother] John obviously doesn't vote. Mark and I vote in every general and most primaries. Washington's vote-by-mail makes it easy. I brought John with me last November when I dropped my ballot in the box at the library and let him 'help' push it in.

follow_ups.question: Will you be raising him to be civically engaged?
follow_ups.response: Definitely. We talk about voting in front of him. He'll grow up knowing it's normal.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: [Mother] John doesn't have political views — he's two. He has strong feelings about which sippy cup is correct. For me and Mark — we're moderate. Mark leans a little more conservative, fiscally; I lean a little more progressive on social stuff. We both voted in the last presidential election but we don't put signs in the yard. We try not to talk politics around John — not because we're hiding it, but because we don't want him repeating things at Little Sprouts. Eastern Washington in general is pretty red, but the Tri-Cities is mixed because of all the Hanford and Energy Northwest workers — lots of scientists and engineers who skew more independent. We're somewhere in that mix.

follow_ups.question: Do you and Mark agree on most things?
follow_ups.response: On 90% of practical things — schools, infrastructure, taxes, yes. On a few hot-button things we disagree, and we just leave it alone.

follow_ups.question: Is there an issue you feel strongest about?
follow_ups.response: Early childhood education funding. I see how much it matters.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: [Mother] Having a kid has shifted me. I care a lot more about local school board races now than I did three years ago. I attended a Kennewick School District board meeting in February about curriculum — first one I've ever been to. Mark has gotten more interested in local utility and infrastructure issues since he started at Energy Northwest. So both of us are more locally focused than we used to be.

follow_ups.question: Any national issues that changed your mind recently?
follow_ups.response: Child care policy. I had opinions before John. Now I have data — and a lot of frustration.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: [Mother] John is too young to have any awareness of this. For Mark and me — somewhat. We're a white family in a fairly white area, so it's not something that touches our daily life. But we read about it, we talk about it privately. I've been thinking about how to talk to John about race as he gets older — we have a few picture books we're slowly working in, like 'All Are Welcome' and 'The Day You Begin.'

follow_ups.question: How do you plan to handle those conversations?
follow_ups.response: Age-appropriately, openly, and without pretending we have all the answers. We want him to be curious and kind.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: [Mother] Mark and I have read about it, talked about it between ourselves. We support the underlying concerns about equal treatment. We're not activists. We try to be thoughtful about who we vote for at the local level — sheriff, prosecutor races matter.

follow_ups.question: Has it changed any specific decisions?
follow_ups.response: Voting choices in our county prosecutor race last cycle.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: [Mother] I think about it in terms of what John will encounter and what we should be teaching him. Kennewick is more diverse than people assume — large Hispanic population especially. Little Sprouts has a mix of kids. We want John to grow up seeing diversity as the default, not the exception.

follow_ups.question: Anyone in his immediate circle from a different background?
follow_ups.response: His friend Ellie at Little Sprouts is from a Mexican-American family, and our neighbors the Hoangs are Vietnamese-American. He plays with their kids all the time and doesn't think twice.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: [Mother] Mostly the first two. Aware, talk privately with Mark and close friends. We didn't attend protests. We donate a small amount yearly to the local food bank and a literacy organization, which is our form of community contribution.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: [Mother] My sister Rachel is more vocal — she went to a march in Spokane. Mark's brother Tim is more conservative and doesn't engage with it. Most of our friends are like us — quietly aware, not on the front lines.

follow_ups.question: Any disagreements that have come up in the family?
follow_ups.response: Mark and Tim had one Thanksgiving where it got heated, then we changed the subject to football and everyone calmed down.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: [Mother] John is a healthy two-year-old. All vaccinations up to date — MMR, DTaP, varicella, hepatitis, the works. He's in the 60th percentile for height, 55th for weight. He's had one ear infection in January, three or four typical colds, no asthma, no allergies that we know of. We see Dr. Reyes at Kadlec Pediatrics every six months for well-visits and she's never raised concerns.

follow_ups.question: Any developmental flags?
follow_ups.response: None. Talking is right on track — he's at about 200 words and putting two and three together. He scored at-age on the M-CHAT screening.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: [Mother] Easy: he's young, he sleeps well (10 hours overnight plus a nap), he eats reasonably, he runs around outside a lot. Hard: he refuses vegetables that aren't carrots or peas — wait, scratch peas, he hates peas. Refuses peas. So we work in vegetables sneakily via smoothies and soups.

follow_ups.question: What about the wildfire smoke last summer?
follow_ups.response: That was hard. We bought a HEPA filter for his room. Now we just keep an eye on AQI forecasts.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: [Mother] Big things — nothing major. The ear infection in January was treated with amoxicillin and resolved in five days. He fell off the couch once at 18 months and we did a precautionary ER visit — totally fine, just a bump. He had a bout of hand-foot-mouth disease from daycare last fall, miserable but uneventful.

follow_ups.question: Was the ER visit stressful?
follow_ups.response: Mark almost passed out. John was fine. It's a Garrity family legend now.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: [Mother] When John was sick with hand-foot-mouth, both Mark and I took days off — Mark used PTO, I used unpaid time. Daycare closed twice last winter for staff illnesses, which scrambled our work weeks.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: [Mother] My mom Linda was diagnosed with mild hypertension last year and is on medication. She's fine. Mark's dad had a knee replacement in 2024 and recovery went well. Nothing has required us to drop everything.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: [Mother] We have good insurance through Mark's job at Energy Northwest. Kaiser-style plan, low copays. John's pediatrics are essentially free at the point of care. We've never had to skip anything. Dental is also covered. We feel very lucky on that front.

follow_ups.question: Anything you wish were easier?
follow_ups.response: Pediatric dentist wait times — six months out for a routine cleaning.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: [Mother] Not really. My mom is into elderberry syrup for colds and we let her give John small amounts because she enjoys it. Otherwise we're conventional medicine people.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: [Mother] John doesn't drink or smoke — he's two. He coped with the daycare-drop-off tears phase by chewing on the strap of his lovey. For me — I have a glass of wine with Mark on Friday nights, sometimes. Nothing more than that.

transcript.question_text: Other people say they cope by relying on prescriptions, pain medications, marijuana, or other substances. How about for you and can you describe your most recent experience of using them, if any?
transcript.response: [Mother] No to all for John. He's had children's Tylenol three or four times for fever, most recently in January with the ear infection. That's the extent of medication.

transcript.question_text: How are you and your family coping with, or paying for, your health care needs right now?
transcript.response: [Mother] Insurance through Mark's employer covers all of us. We have an HSA we contribute to and use for dental and the occasional out-of-pocket cost. Premiums come out of Mark's paycheck pre-tax.

transcript.question_text: Some people are excited about medical vaccination, and others, not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: [Mother] Strongly pro-vaccination. John has every vaccine on the CDC schedule, on time. We don't waver on this.

transcript.question_text: What are your trusted sources of information about the vaccine?
transcript.response: [Mother] Dr. Reyes, our pediatrician. The CDC website. Mark also reads the academic journals via his work access — he's a science-trained guy. We don't get vaccine info from Facebook.

transcript.question_text: Now we're going to talk a bit more about what life was like for you over the past year. Tell me all about how you have been feeling.
transcript.response: [Mother] John has been mostly joyful this year. Big year for him — went from baby to small person. Started preschool, started T-ball, dropped the morning nap. He has tantrums — classic two-year-old stuff — but they're usually short. He's emotionally pretty regulated for his age. He loves big and gets sad big. When his favorite blue blanket went missing for two days in March he was inconsolable.

follow_ups.question: Did you find the blanket?
follow_ups.response: Behind the dryer. Mark has never been so triumphant.

follow_ups.question: What makes him happiest?
follow_ups.response: Tractors and his dad. In that order, depending on the day.

transcript.question_text: Tell me a story about a time in the last year when you were in a rough place or struggling emotionally.
transcript.response: [Mother] The blanket incident in March I just mentioned. Two full days. He'd ask 'Bee-Bee?' (his name for the blanket) and his lip would quiver. He skipped a nap one of those days. We tried decoy blankets, no dice. When we found the original behind the dryer, he hugged it and sobbed.

follow_ups.question: How did he cope?
follow_ups.response: Mostly by clinging to Mark and asking for milky every twenty minutes. Comfort foods and comfort dads.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they struggle with depression, anxiety, or something else like that. How about for you?
transcript.response: [Mother] John, no — not at his age. For me, I had mild postpartum anxiety the first six months. I worked through it with a therapist at Lourdes Counseling. Mark is one of the calmest people on earth. No clinical diagnoses in the household otherwise.

transcript.question_text: How has it been for your family?
transcript.response: [Mother] Stable. We're a pretty even-keel household. My mom takes an antidepressant for low-grade depression and has for a decade — she manages it well.

transcript.question_text: Some people say that religion or spirituality is important in their lives, for others not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: [Mother] We attend Bethel Church in Richland occasionally — non-denominational Christian. Maybe twice a month. We did infant dedication for John there. They have a toddler room he likes — he calls it 'God's room.' Mark grew up Methodist, I grew up Lutheran, we landed at non-denominational by convenience and culture. Religion is part of our family identity but not the center of it.

follow_ups.question: Does John pray at home?
follow_ups.response: We do a simple thank-you prayer before dinner. He folds his hands and says 'amen' loud at the end.

follow_ups.question: Major holidays you celebrate?
follow_ups.response: Christmas and Easter church-wise. Otherwise the standard secular American holidays.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they use Facebook, Instagram, or other social media to stay connected with the wider world. How about for you? Tell me all about how you use these types of platforms.
transcript.response: [Mother] John has no social media presence. We deliberately don't post pictures of his face publicly — only on a private family WhatsApp group with grandparents and aunts/uncles. transcript.question_text: Some people say they use Facebook or Twitter to get (emotional or financial) support during tough times. What about you?

He resides in an owned, middle-class home with two college-educated, married biological parents — Mark, a mechanical engineer in operations support at Energy Northwest, and Sarah, a part-time library aide at Mid-Columbia Library District — placing the household squarely in the dual-income professional middle class of the Tri-Cities region (Q58, Q100, Q101, Q106, Q107). summaries.behavioral_economist: John exhibits an unusually strong preference for routine, predictability, and ordered environments for a child his age — sorting blocks by color and size, lining up his shoes, and reacting with strong loss aversion when his 'Bee-Bee' blanket went missing for two days (Q01, Q03, Q43, Q44). His choice architecture is heavily scaffolded by his parents, who themselves are explicitly spreadsheet-driven decision-makers (sinking funds, 529 plans, four-month emergency fund, deliberate part-time daycare optimization), and these scaffolds appear to be cultivating similar preference patterns in him (Q02, Q03, Q60, Q61).
